new.title: Stand before Chartres Cathedral's blue windows
new.desc: Notre-Dame de Chartres was rebuilt after the fire of 1194 and keeps most of its 12th and 13th-century stained glass, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The nave still holds the famous Chartres blue and the 13th-century labyrinth set in its floor.
new.tip: Entry to the nave is free; the cathedral is generally open from about 8:30 to 19:30. Morning light is best for the west rose and the Blue Virgin window.
new.q: Cathédrale Notre-Dame de Chartres, Cloître Notre-Dame, Chartres

new.title: Descend into the Romanesque crypt of Chartres
new.desc: Beneath the cathedral lies the longest crypt in France, a Romanesque gallery that preserves the foundations of earlier churches and the 11th-century structure of Bishop Fulbert. It holds the chapel of Notre-Dame de Sous-Terre, a place of pilgrimage for centuries.
new.tip: The crypt is visited with a guided tour that starts at the Maison de la Crypte on rue du Cloître Notre-Dame; check the current schedule and book ahead in season.
new.q: Crypte de la cathédrale, Cloître Notre-Dame, Chartres

new.title: Climb the North Tower of Chartres Cathedral
new.desc: The Clocher Neuf, the north tower with its flamboyant Gothic spire from the early 16th century, rises about 115 metres. A climb of roughly 300 steps leads to a gallery above the flying buttresses with views over the old town and the Beauce plain.
new.tip: The tower is a paid visit and is closed in bad weather or at busy times, so check on the day. The queue is shorter at opening time.
new.q: Tour nord, Cathédrale Notre-Dame de Chartres, Cloître Notre-Dame, Chartres

new.title: Marvel at the mosaic Maison Picassiette
new.desc: Raymond Isidore, a cemetery road sweeper, spent decades from 1938 covering his house, garden, chapel and tomb in mosaics made of broken plates and china. It is a major work of outsider art and is listed as a historic monument.
new.tip: Open roughly mid-March to mid-November; check days and prices with the Chartres museums. The house is a short taxi or bus ride from the cathedral.
new.q: Maison Picassiette, 22 rue du Repos, Chartres

new.title: Learn how stained glass is made at the CIV
new.desc: The Centre international du Vitrail occupies a medieval enclosure beside the cathedral's north portal and shows stained-glass art through exhibitions and a gallery. It also runs demonstrations, courses and workshops on glass techniques.
new.tip: Combine it with a look at the cathedral windows; check the centre's site for exhibition hours and workshop dates.
new.q: Centre international du Vitrail, 5 rue du Cardinal Pie, Chartres

new.title: Browse the Musée des Beaux-Arts in the old bishops' palace
new.desc: Housed in the former episcopal palace beside the cathedral, the museum has paintings from the 16th to 20th centuries, Renaissance tapestries and a collection of musical instruments. Its garden terrace overlooks the lower town.
new.tip: Entry is free except during temporary exhibitions; check the City of Chartres page for current opening days.
new.q: Musée des Beaux-Arts, 29 Cloître Notre-Dame, Chartres

new.title: Follow the Chartres en Lumières light trail at night
new.desc: Each evening from spring to the first days of January, around twenty sites in Chartres are lit by animated projections, from the cathedral's royal portal to the bridges, washhouses and churches along the Eure. The festival has run since 2003.
new.tip: Free, from nightfall until late; start at the Église Saint-Pierre and the Pont des Minimes. The 2026 season runs from April, so check the official dates.
new.q: Église Saint-Pierre, Place Saint-Pierre, Chartres

new.title: Walk the Eure from Pont Bouju to Saint-André
new.desc: Below the cathedral, the Eure runs through the lower town past old washhouses, tanneries and mills that worked until the 19th century. The loop from the Pont Bouju to the Collégiale Saint-André is flat and takes about an hour.
new.tip: Free and easy underfoot; come from the Tertre Saint-Nicolas for a low view up at the cathedral.
new.q: Pont Bouju, Rue de la Tannerie, Chartres

new.title: Browse the Marché aux Victuailles on Place Billard
new.desc: Regional producers sell under the Baltard-style iron hall on Place Billard, near the cathedral. The square also hosts a brocante and other events in the year.
new.tip: Wednesday and Saturday mornings, about 7am to 1pm; buy local cheese, charcuterie and fruit for a picnic by the Eure.
new.q: Place Billard, Chartres

new.title: Buy a mentchikoff at La Pâtisserie de Chartres
new.desc: The mentchikoff is a Chartres sweet created in 1893, a Swiss meringue and praline in a chocolate coating. La Pâtisserie de Chartres is listed by the tourist office as a place to find it, with macarons and chocolates.
new.tip: Ask for a box of mentchikoffs to carry home; they keep for a few days.
new.q: La Pâtisserie de Chartres, 2 bis rue du Soleil d'Or, Chartres

new.title: Taste the pâté de Chartres at Le Cochon Dingue
new.desc: The pâté de Chartres is a game pâté in pastry crust, known since the 18th century. Le Cochon Dingue is a charcutier-traiteur on rue de la Pie, listed by Gault&Millau for its local specialities.
new.tip: Buy a slice to take away or eat on the spot; ask which pâté de Chartres is made in-house.
new.q: Le Cochon Dingue, 5 rue de la Pie, Chartres

new.title: Have a coffee at the Café Serpente by the cathedral
new.desc: Le Café Serpente occupies a 16th-century house on the Cloître Notre-Dame, with a terrace facing the south flank of the cathedral and a second entrance on rue des Changes. It serves brasserie meals and coffee all day.
new.tip: Take a table on the terrace for the view of the cathedral, especially at lunch outside the peak rush.
new.q: Le Café Serpente, 2 Cloître Notre-Dame, Chartres

new.title: Look at the Collégiale Saint-André on the Eure
new.desc: The former collegiate church of Saint-André stands on the Eure in the lower town. Its Romanesque and Gothic ruins and arches are lit by projections during Chartres en Lumières, with a view over the river.
new.tip: Free to look at from the riverbank; pair it with the walk from the Pont Bouju.
new.q: Collégiale Saint-André, Rue Saint-André, Chartres

new.title: Tour the Château de Maintenon of Madame de Maintenon
new.desc: The brick-and-stone château on the Eure was bought in 1674 by Françoise d'Aubigné, who later became Louis XIV's secret wife. Its gardens were drawn by Le Nôtre, and the visit includes the royal apartments.
new.tip: Closed on Mondays and with seasonal hours; check the château's site, and the guided tour on weekends.
new.q: Château de Maintenon, Place Aristide Briand, Maintenon

new.title: Look up at the unfinished aqueduct of Maintenon
new.desc: Louis XIV ordered a huge aqueduct in 1685 to bring the water of the Eure to the fountains of Versailles. Work was abandoned in 1688 and only the monumental arches of Vauban and La Hire's project remain.
new.tip: Free to see from the road and riverside; the arches are best seen in the afternoon sun.
new.q: Aqueduc de Maintenon, Pont-Gouin, Maintenon

new.title: Stroll the Le Nôtre gardens of Maintenon
new.desc: Le Nôtre laid out the park of Maintenon at the order of Louis XIV in 1676. The grounds include formal parterres, canals, the Eure and views of the château and the nearby aqueduct.
new.tip: Open longer than the château in high season; summer Saturday evenings sometimes have late opening, so book ahead.
new.q: Jardins du Château de Maintenon, Maintenon

new.title: Climb the keep of the Château de Châteaudun
new.desc: A 31-metre donjon from the late 12th century towers over the Loir above the town. The château also has Gothic and Renaissance wings and, since October 2025, a new visit around Jean de Dunois with a tapestry introduction.
new.tip: Winter hours: 10am to 12:30pm and 2pm to 5:30pm; closed in late June 2026 for a few days. Ten minutes on foot from the station.
new.q: Château de Châteaudun, Place Jean de Dunois, Châteaudun

new.title: Visit Diane de Poitiers' Château d'Anet
new.desc: Henri II gave Anet to Diane de Poitiers, and Philibert de l'Orme built it in the 1540s. Only the central wing, the gate and the chapel remain of what was a masterpiece of the French Renaissance.
new.tip: Guided visit only; open afternoons, closed Tuesdays, and check hours for the season.
new.q: Château d'Anet, Place du Château, Anet

new.title: Sit in Tante Léonie's house at Illiers-Combray
new.desc: Marcel Proust spent childhood holidays in this house in Illiers, which became Combray in In Search of Lost Time. It is now the Musée Marcel Proust, with the aunt's bedroom and the garden of the Pré Catelan nearby.
new.tip: Open Tuesday to Sunday afternoons (longer in July and August); try a madeleine in the town afterwards.
new.q: Maison de Tante Léonie, 4 rue du Docteur Proust, Illiers-Combray

new.title: Visit the Chapelle Royale Saint-Louis at Dreux
new.desc: The royal domain of Dreux holds the Orléans family burial chapel, built in the 19th century on a hill above the town. It is run by the Fondation Saint-Louis and holds the tombs of Louis-Philippe's family.
new.tip: Closed on Tuesdays; guided visits at set times, so check with the tourist office.
new.q: Chapelle royale Saint-Louis, Place Mésirard, Dreux

new.title: Climb the Renaissance belfry of Dreux
new.desc: The 16th-century beffroi of Dreux rises beside the town hall, a Flamboyant Gothic and Renaissance belfry that is a listed monument. A climb up the tower gives a view over the town.
new.tip: Visits are guided and organised by the Dreux tourist office, so check dates; heritage weekend in September includes a visit.
new.q: Beffroi de Dreux, Rue Maurice Viollette, Dreux

new.title: Explore the Château Saint-Jean at Nogent-le-Rotrou
new.desc: The keep was started in the early 11th century by the counts of the Perche, rebuilt under Charles VII and restored in part by Sully. It now houses the Musée de l'histoire du Perche.
new.tip: Ask about the augmented-reality tablet visit; Sully's white marble tomb is behind Notre-Dame church in town.
new.q: Château Saint-Jean, Place Émile Maquaire, Nogent-le-Rotrou

new.title: Walk the moats of Bonneval, the Venice of the Beauce
new.desc: Bonneval keeps medieval gates and fortifications along the Loir, including the 15th-century Porte Saint-Roch with two round towers and the 13th-century Tour du Roi. The river runs through the old moats.
new.tip: Free to walk; electric boat trips on the moats are offered in season.
new.q: Porte Saint-Roch, Rue Saint-Roch, Bonneval

new.title: Lunch at the Brasserie de l'Hôtel de Ville, Nogent-le-Rotrou
new.desc: A relaxed brasserie on the Place Général de Saint-Pol in the centre of Nogent-le-Rotrou, in the Perche. It is a long-standing local address for lunch.
new.tip: Ask for the daily lunch menu; the square is a short walk from the château.
new.q: Brasserie de l'Hôtel de Ville, 30 place Général de Saint-Pol, Nogent-le-Rotrou

new.title: Shop local produce at the Ferme du Porteau
new.desc: A farm shop in a typical Beauce farm at Béville-le-Comte, selling products from local producers of the Terres d'Eure-et-Loir network.
new.tip: Check opening days before you go, as farm shops keep short hours; good for a picnic stock.
new.q: Ferme du Porteau, Béville-le-Comte

new.title: Buy pâté de Chartres at Aux Délices de Saint-Antoine
new.desc: A charcutier-traiteur in Courville-sur-Eure that won a prize of excellence for its pâté de Chartres in 2009, and also makes catering dishes to order.
new.tip: Buy a slice of pâté en croûte to take away; check hours before you go.
new.q: Aux Délices de Saint-Antoine, 58 rue Pannard, Courville-sur-Eure
